books.section: A. The Chesapeake and the Upper South

options.text: Tobacco's growth depended on imported labor and new land, not only on what planters wanted.

options.misconception: The table starts with a first shipment, not a first crop — and 'first' would support the historian, not challenge him.
options.text: Tobacco was the first crop the Chesapeake ever grew, before any other crop was tried.

options.misconception: Three data points cannot show that exports rose every single year without fail.
options.text: Tobacco exports grew steadily through the whole century, rising every single year without fail.

options.misconception: The table says the opposite — tobacco was nearly a third of all British North American exports.
options.text: Tobacco was worthless in England by 1750, and no one there would buy it.

rationales.A: Wanting riches does not explain the system that produced them — the table's scale only makes sense with the labor and land hunger behind it.
rationales.B: The table starts with a first shipment, not a first crop — and 'first' would support the historian, not challenge him.
rationales.C: The table gives only three data points, so it cannot show that exports rose every single year without fail.
rationales.D: The table says the opposite — tobacco was nearly a third of all British North American exports.
rationales.general:
1. Name the claim. One motive — quick riches — explains the whole Chesapeake.
2. Ask what the table needs besides a motive. Thirty-five million pounds a year needs fields, and fields need hands.
3. Bring in the background. Those hands came as indentured servants and enslaved workers, and the fields kept moving to fresh soil.
Remember: a motive is not a system — ask what had to exist for the motive to pay off.

source: original; data table drawn from Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 4
stem: A historian claims that the desire for quick riches alone explains why the Chesapeake developed as it did. Which evidence best challenges that claim?

stimulus.text:
| Year | Tobacco in the Chesapeake |
|---|---|
| 1617 | First shipments sent to England |
| 1700 | More than 35 million pounds exported in a year |
| 1750 | Nearly three-fourths of the Chesapeake's exports, and nearly one-third of all exports from British North America |
